q: For goods under forward charge, time of supply is:
options: Date of invoice, or the last date by which the invoice should have been issued, whichever is earlier
exp: Section 12(2). Advances for goods are no longer taxed for most taxpayers.

q: A supplier receives an advance for goods to be supplied next month. Is GST payable on the advance?
options: Yes, at the time of receipt
No, for most registered persons (other than composition taxpayers), GST on goods is payable at invoice time
exp: Notification 66/2017-CT removed the requirement to pay tax on advances for goods for most taxpayers.

q: A supplier receives an advance for services on 10 March, and the invoice is issued on 5 April. When is GST due on the advance?
options: March, when the advance is received
exp: For services, time of supply is the earliest of invoice date and payment receipt (if the invoice is issued in time). Advances for services are taxable on receipt and reported in GSTR-1 Table 11.

q: A service is completed on 1 June but the invoice isn't issued until 20 July (beyond the 30-day limit). Payment is received on 25 July. Time of supply?
exp: If the invoice isn't issued within the prescribed time, time of supply is the earlier of the date of provision of service and date of payment.

q: Under reverse charge for goods, time of supply is the earliest of:
options: Date of receipt of goods, date of payment, or the date immediately after 30 days from the supplier's invoice
Date of receipt and the 60th day
exp: For RCM goods it's 30 days from the invoice; for services it's 60 days.

q: Under reverse charge for services, time of supply is the earlier of the payment date and:
options: The date immediately after 60 days from the supplier's invoice
exp: Section 13(3). For associated enterprises abroad, it's the earlier of entry in books or payment.

q: If a customer pays up to ₹1,000 more than the invoice amount, the supplier can treat the invoice date as the time of supply for that excess.
exp: This is an option to avoid issuing receipts for tiny excess payments.

q: GST rate on a service changes from 12% to 18% on 1 October. Service provided in September, invoice issued in September, payment received in October. Which rate applies?
exp: Section 14: if supply was before the change and the invoice was issued before it, the old rate applies regardless of later payment. Two of the three events (supply, invoice, payment) fall before the change.

q: For continuous supply of services, when must the invoice be issued if the due date of payment is ascertainable from the contract?
options: On or before the due date of payment
At the start of the contract
exp: Section 31(5)(a).

q: The basic measure of value for GST is:
options: Transaction value, the price actually paid or payable, where parties are unrelated and price is the sole consideration
exp: Section 15(1). Valuation rules apply when those conditions aren't met.

q: Which of these is included in the value of supply?
options: Packing charges and commission charged by the supplier
exp: Incidental expenses like packing and commission are included. GST is excluded, pre-agreed discounts on the invoice are excluded, and government subsidies are excluded.

q: A buyer pays late and is charged ₹2,000 interest by the supplier. GST on the interest?
options: GST at the rate of the original supply
exp: Interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment of consideration is part of the value of supply.

q: A state government gives a manufacturer a subsidy directly linked to the price of its goods. Is it included in the value?
options: No, subsidies from Central and State governments are excluded
Only if shown on the invoice
exp: Subsidies linked to price are included except those provided by the Central and State governments.

q: The buyer pays freight that was the supplier's contractual liability, directly to the transporter. Is it part of the supplier's taxable value?
options: Yes, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid are included
exp: Section 15(2)(b) includes any amount the supplier is liable to pay but which the recipient has incurred and which isn't already in the price.

q: A 5% discount is agreed before the sale and shown on the invoice. Is GST charged on the pre-discount value?
options: No, a discount given before or at the time of supply and recorded on the invoice is excluded
Only if the buyer is registered
exp: Section 15(3)(a).

q: A year-end volume discount is given after supply. When can it reduce the taxable value?
options: When it's per a pre-existing agreement, can be linked to specific invoices, and is issued through a credit note with the recipient reversing the corresponding ITC
exp: Post-supply discounts reduce value only with these conditions. Otherwise it's a commercial credit note that doesn't reduce GST.

q: A financial or commercial credit note (without GST) can be issued for a post-sale discount that doesn't meet the section 15(3) conditions.
exp: The supplier's GST liability stays the same and the recipient doesn't reverse ITC. It's a common practice.

q: A holding company sells goods to its subsidiary (related parties). The subsidiary can claim full ITC. What value is used?
options: The invoice value is deemed to be the open market value
exp: Second proviso to rule 28: where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the invoice value is accepted as open market value. This matters a lot for intra-group cross-charges.

q: Under rule 30 (cost method), value is taken as:
options: 110% of the cost of production, manufacture or acquisition
exp: Rule 30 applies when rules 27 to 29 can't determine value.

q: A dealer in second-hand goods who didn't take ITC on purchase can pay GST on:
options: The margin, selling price minus purchase price (ignored if negative)
exp: Rule 32(5): margin scheme for second-hand goods where no ITC was availed on purchase.

q: A pure agent recovers expenses from the client (e.g. government fees paid on the client's behalf). How are they treated?
options: Excluded, if pure agent conditions in rule 33 are met
exp: Pure agent expenses are excluded when the agent acts under a contract, doesn't hold title, uses the service only on the client's behalf and recovers the exact amount.

q: An Indian branch of a company provides back-office services to its head office in another state without any charge. The head office can claim full ITC. What value should the branch use for GST?
model: Branch and head office in different states are distinct persons, so under Schedule I this is a supply even without consideration. Valuation is under rule 28. Because the recipient is eligible for full ITC, whatever value the branch declares on the invoice is deemed open market value. Circular 199/11/2023 clarified that if the recipient can claim full ITC, even a nil value declared on the invoice is accepted, and for certain components like employee salaries a cross-charge isn't mandatory.
points: Distinct persons, so a supply under Schedule I
Invoice value deemed OMV if full ITC available
exp: Cross-charge between head office and branches is a big practical topic for multi-state companies.

q: For supply of vouchers, how is time of supply generally determined under the original sections 12(4)/13(4)?
options: Date of issue if the supply is identifiable at issue; otherwise date of redemption
exp: The GST Council later recommended that vouchers be treated as neither goods nor services, and the law was amended. Check the current position.

q: Is TCS under income tax included in the value for GST?
options: No, it's an income-tax collection and not part of consideration for supply
exp: CBIC clarified that GST is calculated on value excluding income-tax TCS.

q: Cash discount given for early payment, if known and recorded at the time of the invoice, can be deducted from the taxable value.
exp: If it's agreed before or at the time of supply and shown on the invoice, it's excluded under section 15(3)(a).
